The first focused run found four setup errors from the stale manifest and missing prepared files; the seven completion-control tests already pass. We’re fixing those concrete gaps and checking the runtime integration.

The controller review found substantive gaps: terminal collection leaves the transient service behind, cancellation lacks a cleanup path, and observation results are not bound to the expected service identity. Those fixes take priority over preparing another diagnostic run.

The runtime inputs are also missing from this checkout: the pinned build/source files are absent, and all seven deployment configuration variables are unset. The workers are continuing with controller fixes and an offline preparation path; a live run would currently fail preflight.

The local preparation helper will require explicit, validated inputs and refuse to overwrite an existing package. It will also bind the owner, dispatch, and service identities. That improves preparation and recovery, but it does not by itself satisfy the separate supervisory-lease requirement for a live run.

I flagged another cleanup boundary during review: a failed preflight must not deallocate VMs that this dispatch never started. The tests now cover that case, alongside wrong-owner rejection, failed terminal results, and explicit cancellation.

The workers are implementing the agreed lifecycle changes and the temporary test inputs needed to exercise them. The next review point is whether the focused tests verify safe state transitions—not just whether the generated scripts contain the expected commands.

The first implementation is ready for review, and the offline preparation helper has landed. I found a recovery edge case: if service cleanup succeeds but result upload fails, the next observation must recover the saved terminal result instead of losing it. The workers are adding that fix and a regression test.

Review caught gaps in the new preparation helper too: checking that a source directory exists is not enough to establish its identity. It now needs to verify the tracked contents and pass the controller’s real manifest preflight before publishing a prepared package. I’m keeping that as a completion criterion.

The existing full-check gate is deliberately tied to the retained `effa358f` product build. I’m preserving that boundary rather than relaxing it to make preparation pass. The changes so far are to diagnostic controls and preparation; they do not require a new product benchmark.

The copied tests now build their prepared inputs in temporary directories, so they no longer need a real runtime package to run. Review is also covering recovery after download or cleanup failures, to avoid leaving an otherwise usable result trapped behind a deallocated VM.

The focused suite is down to one failure. It exposed a preflight bug: a substring check mistakes the bounded fingerprint-command timeout for a forbidden product deadline. The fix will distinguish the two while keeping the no-product-deadline rule intact.

The lifecycle fixes are now in place, and the controller worker’s 16 focused checks pass. Terminal results survive upload failures, cancellation is bound to the dispatch owner, and cleanup targets only the validation VM. The remaining work is preparation integration, combined tests, and final review.

All 30 focused tests now pass, and the generated start, observe, and cancel scripts pass shell syntax checks. Final review is tightening two remaining points: recovery must distinguish cancellation from normal completion, and the preparation helper must run the real preflight before calling any output “prepared.”

Peer review found one more preparation bug: the dispatch ID must match the service name, or a package could reuse the wrong result namespace. That fix is going in now. The test fixture leak has also been traced and removed, so tests no longer leave a stray gate file in the checkout.

The combined suite now passes 32 tests. The remaining review findings all concern keeping preparation tied to the intended diagnostic: matching dispatch/service identities, using the exact shared claim path, and preserving the frozen Kubernetes workload. No cloud resources or product runs have been started.

The preparation review uncovered a naming mismatch as well: the workload fingerprint is different from the product source identity. The helper will preserve those existing meanings and reject unsupported inputs. A successful package build remains unverified until the missing retained inputs are available; the failure checks must be clear about that limit.

The executable script review caught a real cache issue: saved terminal status was being trusted before remote cleanup. The controller now validates cached status against the owner, dispatch, and service identity before stopping anything or uploading results. The test worker is checking that ordering with local command stubs.

The lifecycle review is now explicit about recovery: uncertain launches remain available for observation or cancellation; terminal collection can retry from the uploaded archive; and normal completion and cancellation use separate recovery paths. I’m preparing a local commit after the final focused checks, with the missing live inputs and lease requirements documented.
